name: Engineering & Technology
tagline: Design, test, and improve: from first structures to research under uncertainty.

nodes.title: Build, Balance, and Try Again
nodes.goal: Make a small structure, notice what supports it, and improve it after a gentle test.
learning_outcomes: Identify the base and top of a small structure.
Compare two structures after the same gentle test.
Describe one change that made a model work better.

lesson.overview: Engineering begins with making something for a purpose. A toy bridge needs a space underneath and a top that a toy can cross. Blocks touch and support one another; a broad, flat base often makes a small tower steadier than a narrow base. When a model falls, its fall gives us information. We can change one part, try again, and describe what happened without calling the first attempt a failure.
lesson.worked_example: Mina places one wide block on the floor and two small blocks on top. It stands. She puts the wide block at the very top of a narrow tower and it tips during the same gentle tap. She returns the wide block to the base and tests again.
lesson.activity: With an adult, build two low towers from large blocks on the floor. Give each the same gentle tap, draw what happened, then change one tower. Keep blocks away from feet and faces.
lesson.reflection: What did your tower teach you when it fell?

quiz.prompt: Which part of a tower touches the floor?
quiz.explain: The base rests on the floor and supports the parts above it.
quiz.say: Which part of a tower touches the floor?

quiz.prompt: Your block bridge needs a toy car to pass underneath. What must you leave?
quiz.explain: The gap is the space that lets the car pass under the bridge.
quiz.say: Your block bridge needs a toy car to pass underneath. What must you leave?

quiz.prompt: A tower falls. What can a young builder do next?
choices: Change a part and try again
Say no one can build towers
quiz.answer: Change a part and try again
quiz.explain: Trying a change helps us learn which arrangements work.
quiz.say: A tower falls. What can a young builder do next?

quiz.prompt: Which is a fair way to compare two little towers?
choices: Tap both gently in the same way
Push one hard and leave one alone
Use a fan on only one
quiz.answer: Tap both gently in the same way
quiz.explain: Using the same test makes the comparison easier to understand.
quiz.say: Which is a fair way to compare two little towers?

quiz.prompt: Which block is usually a helpful base for a low tower?
choices: A pointed cone standing on its tip
quiz.explain: A wide flat block gives the tower a broad place to rest.
quiz.say: Which block is usually a helpful base for a low tower?

quiz.prompt: The bridge holds one toy. How do you describe what you saw?
choices: It held one toy in this test
It can hold every toy forever
quiz.answer: It held one toy in this test
quiz.explain: One successful test tells us about that test, not every possible load.
quiz.say: The bridge holds one toy. How do you describe what you saw?

nodes.kid_text: Build a little tower. Point to its bottom, called the base. Try a gentle tap. If the tower falls, you can change it and try again. Builders learn by watching!

nodes.title: Tools Help Us Do Things
nodes.goal: Match familiar tools to jobs and describe how a tool changes an action.
learning_outcomes: Match a safe tool to a purpose.
Recognize a ramp and a wheel in toys.
Ask for help before using an unfamiliar tool.

lesson.overview: A tool is something we use to help do a job. A scoop carries loose material, a wheel helps a toy move, and a ramp gives a toy a sloping path. The best tool depends on the task: a soft brush can move sand but cannot hold water like a cup. Engineers watch people using tools and ask what makes the job easier. Young learners can investigate safe toy versions and ask an adult before using an unfamiliar real tool.
lesson.worked_example: A doll needs to move up onto a low book. Lifting the doll goes straight up. Sliding it along a cardboard ramp takes a longer path with a gentler slope. Both paths reach the same book.
lesson.activity: With adult help, move a soft toy onto a low book by hand and then up a cardboard ramp. Say how the two movements differ.
lesson.reflection: Which tool would help you carry sand, and what would you test?

quiz.prompt: Which tool can hold a little water?
quiz.explain: A cup has sides and a bottom that can hold water.
quiz.say: Which tool can hold a little water?

quiz.prompt: A toy car has wheels. What do they help it do?
quiz.explain: Wheels turn as the car moves along a surface.
quiz.say: A toy car has wheels. What do they help it do?

quiz.prompt: Which is a ramp?
quiz.explain: A ramp is a sloping surface that connects different heights.
quiz.say: Which is a ramp?

quiz.prompt: You find a real sharp tool. What is the next step?
quiz.explain: An adult can decide whether a tool is safe and show how it is used.
quiz.say: You find a real sharp tool. What is the next step?

quiz.prompt: A brush cannot carry your water. What should you try?
quiz.explain: A cup can contain water; a brush is made for a different kind of job.
quiz.say: A brush cannot carry your water. What should you try?

quiz.prompt: Why might two people choose different tools?
choices: All tools do exactly the same thing
They may be doing different jobs
Only one person can be right
quiz.answer: They may be doing different jobs
quiz.explain: Tools have different shapes and properties, so different jobs can need different tools.
quiz.say: Why might two people choose different tools?

nodes.kid_text: A tool helps with a job. A cup holds water. Wheels help a toy roll. A ramp slopes up or down. Ask a grown-up before trying a tool you do not know.

nodes.title: Choose Materials for a Job
nodes.goal: Choose a material using observed properties and compare it with an alternative.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish a material from its observable properties.
Use comparable samples in a simple test.
Justify a choice for a specific purpose.

lesson.overview: Materials have properties we can observe: they may be stiff or flexible, absorbent or resistant to water, heavy or light. A useful choice depends on a job rather than a material being best at everything. A sponge helps wipe a spill because it absorbs water, while a container should usually keep water inside. Tests must use comparable pieces and the same amount of water or load. Results describe the samples tested; real products also depend on thickness, shape, and how parts join.
lesson.worked_example: Two equal squares, paper towel and plastic sheet, each receive one spoon of water. The towel becomes wet through; the sheet holds a small puddle. For lining a toy roof, the sheet performed better in this test. For wiping the table, the towel is useful.
lesson.activity: Compare equal pieces of paper, cloth, and foil with an adult. Record bending and a small water-drop test, then choose one for a toy shelter and explain a tradeoff.
lesson.reflection: Could changing a material’s thickness change your decision?

quiz.prompt: Which property helps a towel wipe a spill?
quiz.explain: Absorbent materials take water into spaces within them.
quiz.say: Which property helps a towel wipe a spill?

quiz.prompt: A toy window must let you see through. Which property matters most?
quiz.explain: Transparency means light passes through so you can see objects on the other side.
quiz.say: A toy window must let you see through. Which property matters most?

quiz.prompt: You compare two roof materials. What should stay the same?
choices: The amount of water in each test
quiz.answer: The amount of water in each test
quiz.explain: Using the same amount of water helps compare how the materials behave.
quiz.say: You compare two roof materials. What should stay the same?

quiz.prompt: Why can stiff cardboard still make a weak bridge?
choices: Its shape or supports may be unsuitable
quiz.answer: Its shape or supports may be unsuitable
quiz.explain: The whole design matters, including shape, size, supports, and joints.
quiz.say: Why can stiff cardboard still make a weak bridge?

quiz.prompt: Which is a material rather than a property?
quiz.explain: Wood is a material; flexible and absorbent describe how materials behave.
quiz.say: Which is a material rather than a property?

quiz.prompt: A light material bends too much for your model. What is a useful next step?
choices: Try a folded shape and retest
quiz.answer: Try a folded shape and retest
quiz.explain: Changing the shape can change stiffness without changing the basic material.
quiz.say: A light material bends too much for your model. What is a useful next step?

nodes.kid_text: Think about the job before choosing a material. A towel soaks up water. A clear sheet lets you see through. Try the same small test on each sample and tell someone what you notice.

nodes.title: Ask, Make, Test, Improve
nodes.goal: Turn a small need into criteria, a prototype, a fair test, and a revision.
learning_outcomes: Separate a success criterion from a constraint.
Use a prototype to answer a design question.
Connect an improvement to recorded test results.

lesson.overview: Design starts with someone’s need. Criteria say what success looks like; constraints limit what we may use. A prototype is a model built to answer questions, so it need not look finished. A paper bridge might need to cross a gap and hold three toy animals, using just one sheet of paper. Testing against these criteria is more informative than judging its color. We keep notes so that each revision responds to evidence rather than starting over at random.
lesson.worked_example: A bridge must span 15 cm using one sheet. The flat sheet sags under two toy animals. Folding long edges into rails lets the next version hold three. The new version satisfies the stated load test but still needs a crossing test.
lesson.activity: Design a paper bridge across a short gap between books with adult supervision. State two criteria, sketch two ideas, build one, test with small identical objects, and revise one feature.
lesson.reflection: What evidence would convince another builder that the new version is better?

quiz.prompt: A bridge must hold three toy animals. This is what kind of statement?
quiz.explain: A criterion tells us what the design needs to achieve.
quiz.say: A bridge must hold three toy animals. This is what kind of statement?

quiz.prompt: You may use only one sheet of paper. What is that?
quiz.explain: A constraint limits the resources or choices available.
quiz.say: You may use only one sheet of paper. What is that?

quiz.prompt: Why make a quick prototype?
choices: To find out how an idea works
quiz.answer: To find out how an idea works
quiz.explain: A prototype helps us learn before investing effort in a finished design.
quiz.say: Why make a quick prototype?

quiz.prompt: Version A holds two identical counters; version B holds five. What do these results compare?
choices: How long all bridges will last
quiz.explain: The test measured how many counters each design held under those conditions.
quiz.say: Version A holds two identical counters; version B holds five. What do these results compare?

quiz.prompt: Which note will best help the next attempt?
choices: The third counter bent the middle
quiz.answer: The third counter bent the middle
quiz.explain: A specific observation points to a part or condition that might need changing.
quiz.say: Which note will best help the next attempt?

quiz.prompt: Your bridge holds the toys but blocks the path below. What should happen?
choices: Check it against all the criteria
quiz.answer: Check it against all the criteria
quiz.explain: A design can meet one requirement and miss another, so all relevant criteria matter.
quiz.say: Your bridge holds the toys but blocks the path below. What should happen?

nodes.kid_text: First ask what someone needs. Draw an idea and make a small model. Test it, notice what happens, and change something to help it work better.

nodes.title: Mechanisms and Motion
nodes.goal: Explain how levers, gears, and linkages change the size, direction, or speed of motion.
learning_outcomes: Relate lever arms to ideal force ratios.
Calculate simple gear speed ratios.
Explain a mechanism’s tradeoff between force and distance or speed.

lesson.overview: A mechanism connects moving parts so that an input produces a useful output. A lever turns about a pivot; increasing the effort arm can reduce the force needed for a given load, while the effort moves farther. Meshing gears reverse rotation direction, and different tooth counts exchange rotation speed for torque in an idealized system. Mechanisms do not create energy. Friction and bending mean that real devices lose some input energy to heating and deformation, so ideal calculations are a starting point for testing.
lesson.worked_example: A 12-tooth driving gear turns a 36-tooth gear. When the small gear turns three times, 36 teeth pass the contact point and the large gear turns once in the opposite direction. Ideally the large gear has three times the torque at one-third the rotational speed.
lesson.activity: Use a gear simulation or large toy gears. Predict output direction and turns for equal gears and unequal gears, record observations, and explain where the ideal model simplifies reality.
lesson.reflection: Why does needing less force not mean that a machine supplies free energy?

quiz.prompt: A 10-tooth gear drives a 30-tooth gear. How many driver turns make one output turn?
quiz.explain: Three turns of the 10-tooth gear pass 30 teeth, completing one turn of the larger gear.

quiz.prompt: Two external gears mesh directly. Their rotation directions are usually what?
quiz.explain: Contact pushes one gear clockwise as the other turns counterclockwise.

quiz.prompt: You double a lever’s effort arm while its load arm stays fixed. Ideally the effort force becomes what?
quiz.explain: Balancing moments requires effort times effort arm to equal load times load arm.

quiz.prompt: A machine reduces the force needed to raise a weight. What commonly increases?
quiz.explain: Ideal machines exchange force for distance while conserving work.

quiz.prompt: Why does a real gearbox warm during use?
quiz.explain: Friction converts some mechanical energy to thermal energy.

quiz.prompt: What does a linkage primarily connect?
quiz.explain: Linkages use connected members and joints to guide or transfer motion.

quiz.prompt: A 24-tooth driver makes two turns while meshing with a 12-tooth output. How many turns does the output make?
quiz.explain: The driver passes 48 teeth; the 12-tooth output therefore completes four turns.

quiz.prompt: A lever balances a 6 N load 2 cm from its pivot. What effort balances it at 6 cm?
quiz.explain: Equal moments require effort × 6 = 6 × 2, so effort is 2 N.

quiz.prompt: Adding a third external gear between a driver and an output changes what about their relative direction?
choices: The driver and output alternate direction
The driver and output rotate alike
The driver and output rotate oppositely
quiz.answer: The driver and output rotate alike
quiz.explain: Each gear mesh reverses rotation, so two successive meshes restore the original direction.

quiz.prompt: A linkage’s joint is moved, and the output now follows a different path. What has changed?
choices: The elastic stiffness of the bar material
The mass density of the linked members
quiz.explain: Joint placement changes the permitted relative positions and movement of linked members.

quiz.prompt: A 10-tooth gear drives a 40-tooth gear. Explain the output motion when the driver completes eight turns, including direction and the ideal torque tradeoff.
quiz.answer: The driver passes 80 teeth, so the output makes 2 turns in the opposite direction. Ideally its torque is four times larger while its rotational speed is one quarter, with losses ignored.
quiz.explain: The driver passes 80 teeth, so the output makes 2 turns in the opposite direction. Ideally its torque is four times larger while its rotational speed is one quarter, with losses ignored.

nodes.title: Systems, Sensors, and Feedback
nodes.goal: Represent a simple engineered system using inputs, processes, outputs, and feedback.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish system input, output, and process.
Identify the measurement in a feedback loop.
Explain why sensor errors can affect control.

lesson.overview: A system is a set of parts working together within a chosen boundary. Inputs enter, processes change them, and outputs leave. A controller can use a sensor measurement to compare what is happening with a target. In feedback control, that difference changes an action, which changes the next measurement. A timer alone does not measure the result: watering for one minute is different from watering until a moisture sensor reaches a target. Every sensor has limits, and a misleading measurement can produce an unhelpful response.
lesson.worked_example: A model greenhouse reads 32 degrees while its target is 26. Its controller turns a fan on; later it reads 25 and turns the fan off. The temperature measurement closes the feedback loop. The target is a design choice, not a temperature recommendation for every plant.
lesson.activity: Draw a block diagram for a toy room-temperature controller. Use paper number cards as sensor readings and act out a rule. Include a sensor-failure card and decide what the model should do.
lesson.reflection: Where would you put the system boundary, and what important influence remains outside it?

quiz.prompt: Which part measures temperature in a model greenhouse?
quiz.explain: The sensor supplies a measurement of the system’s condition.

quiz.prompt: What makes feedback different from a fixed timer?
choices: It acts for a preset duration
It runs from an unchanging command
quiz.explain: Feedback uses observed system behavior to adjust future action.

quiz.prompt: A controller compares 18 with a target of 20. What is the target minus measurement?
quiz.explain: The difference is 20 minus 18, or 2; a controller may use this error to choose an action.

quiz.prompt: Which is an output of a toy lamp system?
choices: A command sent by its switch
quiz.explain: Light is a result produced by the lamp system; the command and electrical supply are inputs.

quiz.prompt: A sensor always reports a dry pot even when it is wet. What is a likely concern?
choices: The moisture target may reset itself
quiz.explain: A feedback controller can act on a faulty measurement and make the real condition worse.

quiz.prompt: Why draw a boundary around a system?
choices: To choose controller gains and sensor ranges
To define included parts and external influences
To determine component prices and supply dates
quiz.answer: To define included parts and external influences
quiz.explain: A boundary defines the scope; external influences may still cross it as inputs or disturbances.

quiz.prompt: A fan controller reads air near a cold window instead of the occupied room. What problem should be investigated?
choices: Whether readings represent the occupied space
Whether the target has enough decimal places
Whether the controller averages enough samples
quiz.answer: Whether readings represent the occupied space
quiz.explain: A valid measurement can still be unrepresentative of the condition the system aims to control.

quiz.prompt: A controller turns a lamp on at dusk by measuring outside light. Which item is the actuator?
quiz.explain: An actuator changes the physical system; the sensor measures and the target specifies the desired condition.

quiz.prompt: A timer waters a model plant for a fixed minute without measuring moisture. Which description fits?
quiz.explain: The action does not depend on a measured result, so this is open-loop control.

quiz.prompt: The room warms when a door opens from a hotter corridor. In the room controller model this is what?
quiz.explain: The door introduces an outside influence on temperature rather than a deliberate control command.

quiz.prompt: A model watering controller repeatedly waters an already wet pot because its sensor is beside a dry rock. Explain the problem and one way to investigate it.
quiz.answer: The feedback uses a measurement that may not represent the pot. Compare the sensor reading with independent observations at representative positions, and test whether changing its placement gives a more appropriate measurement before trusting the controller.
quiz.explain: The feedback uses a measurement that may not represent the pot. Compare the sensor reading with independent observations at representative positions, and test whether changing its placement gives a more appropriate measurement before trusting the controller.

nodes.title: Loads, Stress, and Structural Choices
nodes.goal: Analyze simple load paths and use stress and safety factors while stating model assumptions.
learning_outcomes: Trace a load path to supports.
Calculate average axial stress with consistent units.
Distinguish a simplified strength check from a complete safety assessment.

lesson.overview: Loads travel through structural members and connections to supports and foundations. Tension pulls a member, compression pushes it, and bending creates a combination of internal stresses. Average axial stress is force divided by cross-sectional area, but local stress concentrations, buckling, fatigue, and imperfect joints can govern failure. A safety factor compares an appropriate resistance with demand; it is not a guarantee against all hazards. Classroom calculations use idealized geometry and material behavior and do not qualify a design for construction.
lesson.worked_example: A straight bar has cross-sectional area 100 square millimetres and carries 2,000 newtons axially. Average stress is 20 newtons per square millimetre, or 20 MPa. If the stated limit for this simplified check is 60 MPa, the ratio is 3, but the check says nothing yet about connections or repeated loads.
lesson.activity: Analyze a paper truss drawing: mark applied loads, supports, and an estimated load path. Calculate axial stress for two hypothetical areas, then list three reasons a real structure needs more checks.
lesson.reflection: When might adding material fail to solve the actual failure mechanism?

quiz.prompt: A 1,200 N axial load acts on 60 square millimetres. What is average stress?
quiz.explain: Force divided by area gives 20 N per square millimetre, equivalent to 20 MPa.

quiz.prompt: A long slender column fails sideways before crushing. Which mechanism is most relevant?
quiz.explain: Compression can make a slender member lose stability and buckle before the material crushes.

quiz.prompt: Where should a continuous load path ultimately lead?
quiz.explain: For equilibrium, forces must transfer through members and connections into adequate supports.

quiz.prompt: A resistance of 90 units is compared with demand of 30. What is their ratio?
quiz.explain: Resistance divided by demand is 90/30 = 3 for that stated comparison.

quiz.prompt: Why can a hole matter even when average stress is small?
choices: It can reduce the applied load
quiz.explain: Geometry changes can produce local stresses substantially above a section’s average.

quiz.prompt: Which conclusion is warranted by one successful static load test?
choices: It establishes the capacity of future copies
It survived that test’s specified conditions
It will resist a larger repeated loading
quiz.answer: It survived that test’s specified conditions
quiz.explain: A static test alone does not establish behavior under repeated loads, defects, or different conditions.

quiz.prompt: For a fixed axial load, doubling a uniform bar’s cross-sectional area changes average stress how?
quiz.explain: Average axial stress is F/A, so increasing area by a factor of two halves stress.

quiz.prompt: A beam carries a downward load between two supports. Which response is especially relevant?
quiz.explain: The load creates bending within the beam and reactions where the supports restrain it.

quiz.prompt: A part survives one load but cracks after many cycles at the same peak. What should be investigated?
quiz.explain: Fatigue can accumulate damage under repeated loading even below a one-time failure load.

quiz.prompt: Two bars use the same material and area but different connections. Why may their capacities differ?
choices: A joint can govern the assembly’s capacity
The joints determine the material’s density
The joint type rescales the applied force
quiz.answer: A joint can govern the assembly’s capacity
quiz.explain: Connections can introduce local stresses, slip, or weaker load transfer that limits the assembly.

quiz.prompt: A bar carries 3,000 N over 150 square millimetres. Calculate average stress and explain why this alone cannot certify the assembly.
quiz.answer: Average stress is 20 MPa because 3000/150 = 20 N per square millimetre. Connections, local stress concentration, buckling, or repeated loading may govern failure, so the average stress calculation is only one simplified check.
quiz.explain: Average stress is 20 MPa because 3000/150 = 20 N per square millimetre. Connections, local stress concentration, buckling, or repeated loading may govern failure, so the average stress calculation is only one simplified check.

nodes.title: Energy Budgets and Efficient Machines
nodes.goal: Track energy through an engineered device and compare performance within a defined system boundary.
learning_outcomes: Calculate efficiency from an energy budget.
Distinguish power from energy.
Compare designs across explicitly stated lifecycle boundaries.

lesson.overview: An energy budget accounts for inputs, useful outputs, and other transfers over a stated time and boundary. Efficiency is useful output energy divided by input energy, so defining useful output matters. A motor’s heat loss may be undesirable for lifting but useful in a heater. Power is a rate of energy transfer, and lowering power does not necessarily lower total energy if a task takes longer. A design decision can also consider manufacturing, maintenance, and end-of-life impacts rather than concentrating only on use.
lesson.worked_example: A lifting device draws 1,000 joules and raises a load by 700 joules of gravitational potential energy. Its useful-energy efficiency is 70%; the remaining 300 joules go into other transfers such as heat and sound. At 200 watts input it takes five seconds to consume 1,000 joules.
lesson.activity: Build a flow diagram for a fictional motor with a 1,000 J input. Compare two designs by useful output, time, and a separate manufacturing-energy estimate. Keep the units and boundaries visible.
lesson.reflection: How might the preferred design change if it is used once versus a million times?

quiz.prompt: A device produces 80 J of useful output from 100 J input. Its efficiency is what?
quiz.explain: Useful output divided by input is 80/100, or 80%.

quiz.prompt: A 50 W device runs for 20 seconds. How much energy does it use?
quiz.explain: Energy equals power multiplied by time: 50 joules per second times 20 seconds.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about a lower-power motor is justified by power alone?
choices: It finishes a fixed task in less time
It transfers energy at a lower rate
It uses less energy for the whole task
quiz.answer: It transfers energy at a lower rate
quiz.explain: Power is a rate; total energy also depends on operating time.

quiz.prompt: Why specify the system boundary in an efficiency comparison?
quiz.explain: A comparison can be misleading if one boundary includes losses that another omits.

quiz.prompt: Which transfer may be useful for a heater but a loss for a lift?
choices: Energy stored in the raised load
quiz.explain: Useful output depends on the intended service, so room heating can be desired in one system.

quiz.prompt: A product saves energy during use but requires much more to manufacture. What helps judge the tradeoff?
quiz.explain: Use over the product’s lifetime determines whether operational savings outweigh initial energy costs.

quiz.prompt: Device A uses 100 W for 10 s; B uses 50 W for 30 s. Which uses less energy?
quiz.explain: A consumes 1,000 J and B consumes 1,500 J, so A uses 500 J less despite its higher power.

quiz.prompt: A motor outputs 60 J of useful work from 75 J input. What is its efficiency?
quiz.explain: Efficiency is 60/75 = 0.8, expressed as 80%.

quiz.prompt: An energy diagram lists 500 J input and 450 J output but no storage change. What needs attention?
choices: Rescale output units until the totals match
Check omitted transfers and storage terms
Assign the residual to destroyed energy
quiz.answer: Check omitted transfers and storage terms
quiz.explain: Conservation requires accounting for all transfers and storage; a residual may reflect omitted terms or measurement error.

quiz.prompt: Manufacturing consumes 600 J more for a design that saves 20 J per use. When is the energy difference recovered?
quiz.explain: With the stated constant savings and boundary, 600/20 = 30 uses reaches break-even.

quiz.prompt: Device A uses 150 W for 20 s, while B uses 100 W for 40 s to perform the same task. Compare energy use and explain the role of power.
quiz.answer: A uses 3000 J and B uses 4000 J. Energy is power multiplied by time, so the higher-power device A uses less total energy here because it finishes sooner.
quiz.explain: A uses 3000 J and B uses 4000 J. Energy is power multiplied by time, so the higher-power device A uses less total energy here because it finishes sooner.

nodes.title: Dynamic Models and Feedback Design
nodes.goal: Model a first-order process, analyze proportional feedback, and examine stability and measurement limitations.
learning_outcomes: Derive a basic closed-loop transfer function.
Predict steady-state error and time constant for a stated model.
Evaluate effects of delay, noise, and actuator constraints.

lesson.overview: Dynamic models connect inputs to how a state changes with time. A first-order plant can be written tau times dx/dt plus x equals K times u, with time constant tau and static gain K. Feedback compares a measured output with a reference, and a proportional controller multiplies the error by a gain. Increased gain may reduce steady-state error and speed a simple response, but delays, actuator limits, noise, and unmodeled dynamics can undermine the design. Validation therefore uses time traces and disturbances, not just a tidy transfer function.
lesson.worked_example: For a unit-gain plant with time constant 4 seconds and proportional gain 3 under unity feedback, the closed-loop transfer is 3/(4s+4). Its time constant is 1 second and its steady output for a unit step is 0.75, leaving error 0.25. These results assume no delay or saturation.
lesson.activity: Simulate the stated first-order model at gains 1, 3, and 9. Plot reference, output, and control effort; then add a measurement delay or actuator cap and discuss where the simple prediction becomes insufficient.
lesson.reflection: Which observations would persuade you that the plant model needs revision rather than more controller tuning?

quiz.prompt: For G(s)=1/(4s+1) and proportional gain 3, what is the unity-feedback closed-loop transfer?
quiz.explain: The closed-loop expression is 3G/(1+3G), which simplifies to 3/(4s+4).

quiz.prompt: What is the unit-step steady-state output of 3/(4s+4)?
quiz.explain: For this stable system the DC gain is 3/4, so the unit-step output tends to 0.75.

quiz.prompt: Which observation directly challenges a no-delay model?
choices: A repeatable exponential rise in output
A repeatable wait before output begins
A repeatable final output near the target
quiz.answer: A repeatable wait before output begins
quiz.explain: A repeatable delay before response indicates dynamics absent from an instantaneous-input model.

quiz.prompt: Why inspect control effort as well as output?
choices: It may exceed the actuator’s available range
It may redefine the reference input’s units
It may conceal the plant’s geometric scale
quiz.answer: It may exceed the actuator’s available range
quiz.explain: Saturation can change the actual closed-loop behavior and invalidate an unconstrained calculation.

quiz.prompt: What can high proportional gain do to sensor noise in the commanded action?
choices: Convert noise into a fixed bias
quiz.explain: The controller multiplies measured error, including its noise component, by the gain.

quiz.prompt: What is the time constant of 3/(4s+4)?
quiz.explain: Dividing numerator and denominator by 4 gives 0.75/(s+1), whose time constant is 1.

quiz.prompt: For a unit-gain first-order plant and proportional gain 9 under unity feedback, what is unit-step steady error?
quiz.explain: The static closed-loop gain is 9/(1+9)=0.9, leaving steady error 0.1.

quiz.prompt: A controller performs well in simulation but oscillates with a real communication lag. Which next model change is most relevant?
quiz.explain: Delay introduces phase effects that can change stability and should be represented and tested.

quiz.prompt: A constant sensor bias persists after averaging many readings. What explains this?
choices: Averaging changes the true system state
quiz.explain: Repeated samples can reduce random noise while leaving calibration bias unchanged.

quiz.prompt: A controller requests 12 units but its actuator is capped at 5. What input reaches the plant?
quiz.explain: The actuator constraint limits applied input to 5; the unconstrained command is not the delivered action.

quiz.prompt: For G(s)=1/(2s+1) with proportional gain 4 and unity feedback, derive the closed-loop transfer and unit-step steady error. State one omitted real-world effect.
quiz.answer: The closed-loop transfer is 4/(2s+5), giving DC gain 0.8 and unit-step steady error 0.2. This calculation omits effects such as sensor delay, actuator saturation, and model mismatch, any of which may change actual performance.
quiz.explain: The closed-loop transfer is 4/(2s+5), giving DC gain 0.8 and unit-step steady error 0.2. This calculation omits effects such as sensor delay, actuator saturation, and model mismatch, any of which may change actual performance.

nodes.title: Reliability, Experiments, and Tradeoffs
nodes.goal: Estimate simple system reliability and design experiments that distinguish effects from uncontrolled variation.
learning_outcomes: Calculate simple independent series and parallel reliabilities.
Identify common-cause and dependence assumptions.
Design a replicated, randomized comparison with explicit factors.

lesson.overview: Reliability is the probability of performing a defined function for a specified time under stated conditions. In a series system every required component must work, so independent component reliabilities multiply. Redundancy can help, but a shared power loss or environmental hazard creates common-cause failures that independence calculations miss. Engineering experiments use replication to estimate variation, randomization to reduce systematic bias, and blocking to account for known nuisance factors. Design tradeoffs should compare performance, cost, maintainability, and uncertainty, rather than treating a single mean result as decisive.
lesson.worked_example: Two independent required components each have reliability 0.9 over the same mission. Series reliability is 0.81. Two independent parallel components, either of which can complete the mission, have reliability 1 minus 0.1 squared, or 0.99; this assumes the switching and shared supplies do not introduce extra failures.
lesson.activity: Plan a small factorial experiment comparing two paper-fold patterns and two paper thicknesses. Randomize trial order, use multiple specimens per condition, and explain why retesting the same damaged specimen is not an independent replicate.
lesson.reflection: Which shared cause could make an apparently redundant system much less reliable?

quiz.prompt: Two independent required components each have reliability 0.8. What is series reliability?
quiz.explain: Both must succeed, so independence gives 0.8 times 0.8 = 0.64.

quiz.prompt: Two independent backup units each fail with probability 0.1. If either working unit suffices, what is system reliability?
quiz.explain: Both must fail for system failure: 0.1 times 0.1 = 0.01, leaving reliability 0.99.

quiz.prompt: Both backup pumps use one power supply. What does this introduce?
quiz.explain: Failure of the shared power supply can disable both pumps together.

quiz.prompt: Why randomize the order of material tests?
choices: Increase the strength of each specimen
Reduce the number of required specimens
quiz.explain: Random order reduces systematic association between treatment and trends such as room temperature or operator fatigue.

quiz.prompt: What does replication help estimate?
choices: The specific direction of allocation bias
The exact response of an untested design
quiz.explain: Repeated independent units reveal how variable outcomes are under a given condition.

quiz.prompt: A two-factor design tests both shape and thickness. What is an interaction?
choices: Shape and thickness have additive effects
Shape and thickness have equal effects
quiz.explain: An interaction means one factor’s effect changes across levels of another factor.

quiz.prompt: A study compares designs by testing one only in winter and the other only in summer. What weakens the inference?
quiz.explain: Seasonal conditions may explain the observed difference instead of design.

quiz.prompt: A component has reliability 0.95 over one month. Can this be reused as its reliability over ten years without a model?
choices: Yes; the component design is unchanged
Yes; scale the probability by duration
quiz.explain: Reliability is tied to a specified mission and conditions; transfer across time requires a justified model.

quiz.prompt: In a factorial test, a fold helps thin paper but hurts thick paper. What does this support?
choices: A sampling error established by definition
A constant effect of fold geometry
quiz.explain: The direction or size of one factor’s effect depends on the other factor.

quiz.prompt: A backup unit works, but the switch fails to connect it. What was missing from the simple reliability model?
choices: The reliability of the switching mechanism
The reliability of the load’s measurement
The reliability of the operator’s schedule
quiz.answer: The reliability of the switching mechanism
quiz.explain: A redundant architecture relies on supporting components whose failures must be considered.

quiz.prompt: Two backup units each have reliability 0.8 and either can complete a mission. Calculate ideal system reliability and critique the calculation if they share one power supply.
quiz.answer: Under independence, both fail with probability 0.2 times 0.2 = 0.04, giving reliability 0.96. A shared power supply can create a common-cause failure, violating independence and requiring a more complete system model.
quiz.explain: Under independence, both fail with probability 0.2 times 0.2 = 0.04, giving reliability 0.96. A shared power supply can create a common-cause failure, violating independence and requiring a more complete system model.

nodes.title: Robust Optimization and Design Under Uncertainty
nodes.goal: Formulate and critique a constrained design optimization with uncertain inputs, sensitivity analysis, and competing objectives.
learning_outcomes: Formulate constrained and multi-objective design problems.
Distinguish nominal, robust, and probabilistic uncertainty treatments.
Critique model validity using sensitivity, validation, and reproducible reporting.

lesson.overview: Engineering optimization selects design variables to improve objectives while respecting constraints. A nominal optimum assumes a particular input set; a robust formulation asks how it performs across a defined uncertainty set, while chance constraints use an explicit probability model. Neither approach makes uncertainty disappear. A Pareto frontier identifies designs where improving one objective requires worsening another. Graduate analysis must defend the uncertainty model, distinguish numerical convergence from a credible physical model, and test whether conclusions survive plausible changes in assumptions and stakeholder priorities.
lesson.worked_example: Three fictional designs have cost and worst-case deflection pairs (10,8), (12,5), and (14,9). The third is dominated because the first is both cheaper and less deflected. The first two are non-dominated; selecting between them requires a limit or preference. If load uncertainty increases, those deflection values must be recomputed rather than reused.
lesson.activity: Write a reproducible optimization study for a simulated beam or resource network. State variables, units, objective, constraints, uncertainty set, solver settings, and validation checks. Compare nominal and robust solutions, then critique one assumption with a sensitivity study and a limitation statement.
lesson.reflection: Whose preferences define the objective, and which harms or costs are omitted from it?

quiz.prompt: Design A costs 10 with deflection 8; design B costs 14 with deflection 9. Both are minimized. Which is true?
quiz.explain: A is better in both objectives, so B is dominated under these stated metrics.

quiz.prompt: What does a robust constraint typically require?
choices: Feasibility at the average input value
Feasibility under the fitted output curve
Feasibility over a specified input set
quiz.answer: Feasibility over a specified input set
quiz.explain: Robustness is defined relative to the chosen set; it is not universal protection.

quiz.prompt: A chance constraint permits failure probability at most 0.01. What is essential to interpret it?
choices: The objective’s name and parameter count
The selected optimizer and display settings
quiz.explain: The probability claim depends on how uncertain inputs and their dependence are modeled.

quiz.prompt: A solver converges precisely on an inaccurate physical model. What follows?
choices: A precise solution can remain physically wrong
A precise solution confirms the physical model
A precise solution removes validation uncertainty
quiz.answer: A precise solution can remain physically wrong
quiz.explain: Numerical solution accuracy does not establish the validity of the model being solved.

quiz.prompt: Why report a Pareto frontier rather than only a weighted score?
choices: To replace priorities with one numerical ordering
To infer priorities directly from solver settings
To reveal alternatives under competing priorities
quiz.answer: To reveal alternatives under competing priorities
quiz.explain: The frontier preserves competing outcomes instead of hiding them within a single weighting.

quiz.prompt: The preferred design changes under a small plausible parameter shift. What should the report emphasize?
choices: The best-case input and its favorable ranking
The original optimum and its extra precision
quiz.explain: A fragile preference is a substantive finding and should shape the conclusion.

quiz.prompt: A robust solution is expensive because its uncertainty set includes physically incompatible extremes together. What should be reviewed?
choices: The joint uncertainty set and its dependence
The decision variable names and their ordering
The plotted axes and their visual proportions
quiz.answer: The joint uncertainty set and its dependence
quiz.explain: A poorly justified set may be excessively conservative; dependence and feasibility of joint extremes need examination.

quiz.prompt: Two equally weighted objectives have units of dollars and millimetres. What is a concern?
choices: Weights depend on units and scaling
quiz.answer: Weights depend on units and scaling
quiz.explain: A raw weighted sum embeds unit-sensitive tradeoffs that require deliberate normalization or justified weights.

quiz.prompt: A chance-constrained design passes under independent loads but fails when load correlations are introduced. What should change?
choices: Exclude correlated scenarios as numerical outliers
Reassess load dependence and resulting risk
Retain the independent model for comparability
quiz.answer: Reassess load dependence and resulting risk
quiz.explain: Joint dependence affects tail events and constraints, so it is part of the uncertainty model.

quiz.prompt: An optimizer returns a feasible local solution to a nonconvex problem. Which report is defensible?
choices: A local result with stated search limits
A global optimum from convergence alone
A proof that feasible alternatives do not exist
quiz.answer: A local result with stated search limits
quiz.explain: Local convergence does not prove global optimality in a nonconvex problem.

quiz.prompt: An optimized design is feasible at mean load but violates its limit in a plausible high-load scenario. Propose a revised analysis and explain what it would and would not establish.
quiz.answer: Compare the nominal solution with a robust design over a justified uncertainty set, or use a probability model for a chance constraint. Perform sensitivity analysis on loads and dependence. Feasibility is conditional on those assumptions and model validity, not a guarantee against unspecified events.
quiz.explain: Compare the nominal solution with a robust design over a justified uncertainty set, or use a probability model for a chance constraint. Perform sensitivity analysis on loads and dependence. Feasibility is conditional on those assumptions and model validity, not a guarantee against unspecified events.

nodes.title: Verification, Validation, and Engineering Research
nodes.goal: Design a defensible engineering research study that separates code verification, model validation, uncertainty, and generalization.
learning_outcomes: Separate numerical verification from empirical validation.
Prevent calibration data from masquerading as independent validation.
Design and critique a reproducible research protocol with uncertainty and scope limits.

lesson.overview: Verification asks whether the equations were solved correctly; validation asks whether a model is sufficiently representative for its intended use. Agreement with calibration data is not independent evidence of predictive performance. A research study defines a quantity of interest, measurement uncertainty, validation conditions, and acceptance criteria before interpreting results. Mesh refinement, analytic benchmarks, holdout experiments, and discrepancy analysis answer different questions. Graduate work also documents provenance, failed hypotheses, and limits of transfer so another team can reproduce the analysis and judge where the result should not be used.
lesson.worked_example: A thermal model is fitted to three heating trials and matches them closely. A fourth trial at a new airflow produces a systematic temperature error. A smaller numerical time step barely changes predictions. The evidence points toward missing physics or parameter transfer limits, rather than merely time-discretization error.
lesson.activity: Propose a research protocol for a low-risk simulated or tabletop system: separate calibration and validation cases, prerecord success metrics, quantify sensor and numerical uncertainty, and include a negative result. Produce an executable notebook or detailed calculation record plus a critique of generalization.
lesson.reflection: What evidence would falsify the explanation you currently prefer?

quiz.prompt: A numerical solver reproduces a known analytic solution. This mainly supports what?
quiz.explain: An analytic benchmark tests whether the numerical method solves the intended equations correctly.

quiz.prompt: Why reserve validation cases that were not used for fitting?
choices: To improve agreement on the fitting cases
To choose parameters from their best outcomes
To test prediction beyond the fitting cases
quiz.answer: To test prediction beyond the fitting cases
quiz.explain: Independent cases reduce the risk of mistaking a good fit for predictive validity.

quiz.prompt: Halving the time step barely changes a prediction that disagrees with experiment. What is reasonable?
choices: Examine model form, inputs, and measurements
Attribute the error directly to time resolution
quiz.answer: Examine model form, inputs, and measurements
quiz.explain: Small discretization sensitivity shifts attention to other sources of discrepancy without proving which one dominates.

quiz.prompt: What should an acceptance criterion specify?
choices: An intended-use metric with a stated tolerance
A visual resemblance judged after calibration
A target result chosen after viewing predictions
quiz.answer: An intended-use metric with a stated tolerance
quiz.explain: A predefined metric and tolerance make evaluation interpretable and reduce post-hoc goal changes.

quiz.prompt: Two sensors share the same calibration bias. Why can treating their errors as independent mislead?
choices: A common bias shrinks with sample count alone
A common bias increases instrument resolution
A common bias can remain after averaging
quiz.answer: A common bias can remain after averaging
quiz.explain: Common systematic error persists across measurements and changes uncertainty propagation.

quiz.prompt: A model validated at low loads is proposed for extreme loads. What is needed?
choices: A finer plot of predictions at the old regime
Evidence for transfer to the new load regime
A relabeling of the original validation dataset
quiz.answer: Evidence for transfer to the new load regime
quiz.explain: Validation is tied to conditions and purpose; new regimes may involve different mechanisms.

quiz.prompt: A model’s prediction improves after validation cases are repeatedly used to tune parameters. What happens to those cases?
choices: They remove the need for holdout cases
quiz.explain: Repeated tuning uses information from the cases, weakening their independence as a final validation test.

quiz.prompt: Measurement and model prediction have uncertainty bands that overlap. What can be concluded from overlap alone?
choices: Overlap establishes adequacy in the tested use
Overlap identifies the source of model error
Overlap alone does not establish adequacy
quiz.answer: Overlap alone does not establish adequacy
quiz.explain: Adequacy depends on metrics, tolerances, uncertainty structure, and intended decisions, not visual overlap alone.

quiz.prompt: A mesh-refinement study changes the output materially at each refinement. What is unresolved?
quiz.explain: Strong refinement dependence suggests numerical resolution has not stabilized for the quantity of interest.

quiz.prompt: A validation experiment deliberately probes where two models disagree most. What is its value?
choices: It can separate competing model predictions
It can fit both models with the same constants
It can remove uncertainty from both predictions
quiz.answer: It can separate competing model predictions
quiz.explain: Informative experimental conditions can distinguish models that behave similarly under routine conditions.

quiz.prompt: A simulation is calibrated to three trials, matches them, and misses a fourth trial. Mesh refinement changes predictions negligibly. Explain the different evidence and next research step.
quiz.answer: Calibration fit is not independent validation. Mesh refinement supports numerical verification for the quantity examined, while the fourth trial exposes predictive discrepancy. Investigate measurement uncertainty, input assumptions, and model form, then test a revised hypothesis on independent cases.
quiz.explain: Calibration fit is not independent validation. Mesh refinement supports numerical verification for the quantity examined, while the fourth trial exposes predictive discrepancy. Investigate measurement uncertainty, input assumptions, and model form, then test a revised hypothesis on independent cases.
